thread.title: As the GOP tax plan became law, we reported on Apple's likel

author: Feria Investor
title: As the GOP tax plan became law, we reported on Apple's likel
text:
As the GOP tax plan became law, we reported on Apple's likely $40bn tax bill resulting from the deemed repatriation provisions of the law. While many investors speculated on how Apple ( AAPL ) would spend its over $250bn in cash and securities now that it would be subject to the tax, from special dividends to paying down debt to wishful acquisitions , the company did us all a favor by announcing some special news regarding its cash pile. 
Apple claims it will spend up to $350bn over the next few years investing in America. It will seek to hire 20,000 workers as part of this expansion. This figure includes the $38bn in deemed repatriation taxes owed under the new bill, noting "a payment of that size would likely be the largest of its kind ever made."
Planned capital expenditures in the US, investments in American manufacturing over five years and a record tax payment upon repatriation of overseas profits will account for approximately $75 billion of Apple's direct contribution.
Importantly, Apple seeks to open a new campus to accommodate the new influx of personnel under this plan. The location of this new campus, still a mystery, will likely be the subject of Amazon-like lobbying by governors, mayors and legislatures alike. 
Stock Bonuses Apple also is undertaking a bonus of $2,500 of restricted stock to most Apple employees, another feature of its announcement today. It has joined the likes of AT&T ( T ) and other companies that have announced bonuses resulting from the GOP tax cut plan enacted at the end of 2017. 
What About the Balance Sheet? Shockingly absent from this congratulatory press release is any indication that any debt will be retired (unlikely), how the share repurchase program would be affected, or if the quarterly dividend will be increased. Apple currently has around $270bn in cash and securities, with roughly $250bn stashed overseas. It recently issued another $7bn in debt to help finance the capital return program, as the overseas funds had not at the time been subject to the new tax laws. 
The new GOP tax bill deems Apple's overseas cash as if it has been repatriated, rendering the $38bn tax bill Apple announced today. With $350bn slated to be spent under these capital expenditure plans, it seems likely Apple will once again tap the debt markets even as its free cash flow remains robust (Apple's trailing 12-month cash flow ending September 2017 was $50bn). With a dividend and repurchase program remaining intact for the foreseeable future, we expect Apple to slowly roll out these expenditures over the expected time frame as it may not be a good idea to rush to spend. 
Additionally, the company customarily announces changes to its capital return program in April of every year. With its first earnings call of the year occurring February 1, 2018, we expect analysts on the call to question Apple's ability to withstand these capital expenditures as its core businesses continue to generate large amounts of free cash flow.
